title: When Not to Use Kubernetes
description: Learn to recognize when Kubernetes introduces more complexity than value, and explore simpler deployment alternatives for C# applications.

data.text: Kubernetes has become the default answer to 'how should we deploy our application?' But Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform, not a deployment simplification layer. It provides powerful capabilities: auto-scaling, service discovery, rolling updates, and self-healing. It also demands significant expertise: networking configuration, resource management, secret handling, storage orchestration, and cluster lifecycle management. For many C# applications, a simpler platform delivers the same result with a fraction of the operational burden.

An ASP.NET Core application packaged as a Docker container can run on virtually any host. Before committing to Kubernetes, consider whether the application actually needs the features Kubernetes provides. If the answer is no, the team is paying a complexity tax without receiving the benefits.

data.title: Red flags for Kubernetes adoption
items: The application is a single service with predictable traffic. A single VM or App Service is simpler and cheaper.
The team has no dedicated DevOps or platform engineer. Kubernetes is a full-time job, not a side project.
Stateful workloads dominate. Databases, message queues, and file stores require careful Kubernetes configuration and often run better on managed services.
The deployment frequency is low. Kubernetes shines with frequent, automated deployments. If you deploy monthly, the orchestration overhead is wasted.
Compliance or data residency requirements forbid multi-tenant cluster models.

data.title: Kubernetes solves organizational problems
data.text: Kubernetes is rarely the right answer for a single team with a single application. It becomes valuable when you have dozens of services, multiple teams, and a need for standardized deployment patterns. If you are not at that scale, you are solving tomorrow's problem at today's expense.

rows: Standard web apps and APIs with moderate traffic
Native deployment slots, staging, and diagnostics
Direct Docker support, KEDA scaling, no YAML required
Containerized or .NET Framework apps on AWS

data.text: A common anti-pattern is moving an application to Kubernetes simply because the organization has adopted Kubernetes elsewhere. This is lift-and-shift: moving an application to a new platform without redesigning it for that platform. The application does not gain auto-scaling, resilience, or service discovery benefits because it was not architected to use them. It only gains operational complexity.

data.title: Deploying an ASP.NET Core app the simple way
data.content: A minimal Dockerfile for an ASP.NET Core API that can run on any container host, including Kubernetes but also simpler platforms.
data.code:
# Build stage
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["MyApi.csproj", "./"]
RUN dotnet restore "./MyApi.csproj"
COPY . .
RUN dotnet build "./MyApi.csproj" -c Release -o /app/build

RUN dotnet publish "./MyApi.csproj" -c Release -o /app/publish /p:UseAppHost=false

# Runtime stage
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/publish .
EXPOSE 8080
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "MyApi.dll"]

data.text: Kubernetes is appropriate when you have many services, need dynamic scaling based on custom metrics, run multi-tenant workloads, or require high availability across zones. It is also appropriate when the organization has the platform engineering expertise to manage it. If you meet these criteria, Kubernetes is a powerful tool. If you do not, it is an expensive distraction.

items.question: Can we start simple and move to Kubernetes later?
items.answer: Yes. Containerize your application correctly from the start, using environment variables for configuration and health checks for liveness. This makes the eventual migration to Kubernetes much easier because the application is already container-friendly.

items.question: Is Azure Container Apps a good middle ground?
items.answer: For many .NET teams, yes. Azure Container Apps provides Kubernetes-like scaling and traffic management without requiring you to manage clusters directly. It is a good stepping stone between App Service and full Kubernetes.

items.question: What about Kubernetes at the edge or on-premises?
items.answer: Kubernetes can make sense in these scenarios when you need consistent deployment patterns across distributed sites. But even then, evaluate edge-specific distributions like K3s or managed Kubernetes offerings that reduce operational overhead.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Kubernetes is powerful but operationally expensive; it is not a default deployment choice.
Simpler platforms like App Service or Container Apps often deliver the same business value.
Lift-and-shift to Kubernetes without architectural changes adds complexity without benefits.
Evaluate Kubernetes only when you have the scale, team expertise, and operational maturity to justify it.
data.takeaway: Choose the simplest platform that meets your actual requirements. Senior engineers do not adopt Kubernetes because it is trendy; they adopt it because the application genuinely needs orchestration at scale.
